label: Symplectic Manifolds
notes: Open by framing the chapter's thesis: Hamiltonian mechanics is not really about a metric or a Lagrangian but about an oriented area form on phase space. Promise the learner that by the end they will see the bracket, the flow, and Darboux's theorem all flow from one closed nondegenerate two-form omega.

label: The Symplectic Form
notes: Define a symplectic manifold carefully as an even-dimensional manifold carrying a closed nondegenerate two-form. Stress that nondegeneracy forces even dimension and gives an isomorphism between vectors and covectors, while closedness is the integrability condition that will later make the Poisson bracket satisfy Jacobi.

label: Cotangent Bundle Example
notes: Walk through the canonical example: the cotangent bundle of configuration space. Emphasize that the tautological one-form theta exists on any cotangent bundle without extra choices, and that omega equals minus d theta is automatically closed and nondegenerate, so every mechanical phase space is symplectic for free.

label: Measuring Oriented Area
notes: Make the geometry concrete: omega is a sum of oriented areas, one per conjugate plane. Show how feeding two vectors into omega returns the signed area of the parallelogram they span, projected onto each q-p plane. This area interpretation is what the flow will later preserve.

label: Hamiltonian Vector Fields
notes: This is the central correspondence of the chapter. Given a function H, nondegeneracy lets us invert omega to turn the covector dH into a vector field X_H. Describe it as a ninety degree rotation of the gradient, so X_H is tangent to level sets of H, which is why energy is conserved.

label: The Flow Picture
notes: Connect the algebra to motion. Integral curves of X_H are exactly the solutions of Hamilton's equations. Point out that because X_H is built from the symplectic form, the resulting flow automatically preserves omega, foreshadowing Liouville and the integral invariants discussed two slides later.

label: The Poisson Bracket
notes: Introduce the Poisson bracket as the pairing of two Hamiltonian fields through omega. Highlight the three structural facts: antisymmetry, the Leibniz product rule, and the Jacobi identity, which holds precisely because omega is closed. Note that f evolves in time by its bracket with H.

label: Darboux's Theorem
notes: State Darboux's theorem and explain its philosophical weight: unlike Riemannian geometry there is no local curvature invariant. Every symplectic manifold looks identical near a point, so all local symplectic geometry is the standard model. Differences between symplectic manifolds are entirely global, not local.

label: Canonical Transformations
notes: Define canonical or symplectic transformations as diffeomorphisms preserving omega. Stress that these are exactly the changes of coordinates under which Hamilton's equations keep their form, and that they form a group. This invariance is the deep reason canonical coordinates are interchangeable in mechanics.

label: Generating Functions
notes: Show how generating functions produce canonical transformations implicitly. A function S of mixed old and new coordinates yields the transformation by partial differentiation. Emphasize this is the bridge to Hamilton-Jacobi theory and explains why the action functional generates the flow itself.

label: Integral Invariants
notes: Present the Poincare integral invariants as the conserved quantities of the flow. The loop integral of p dq and the area integral of omega are preserved along the Hamiltonian flow. Mention that the top power of omega is the Liouville volume, recovering conservation of phase volume.

label: Synthesis
notes: Close by drawing the whole chapter together: one closed nondegenerate form generates fields, brackets, flows, and invariants. Recap that the symplectic form is the single object from which all of Hamiltonian mechanics unfolds, and preview that integrable systems exploit this structure through action-angle coordinates.
